findings.title: The divine names as invocation
findings.claim: The opening phrase can be heard as invoking God through the named titles: the wider wording of 17:110 explicitly places calling on Allah and calling on al-Rahman alongside God's beautiful names.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries the ordinary noun اسم, ‘name,’ in بِسْمِ. In 17:110, the instruction names Allah and al-Rahman as forms of address and says that His are the beautiful names. Their contact gives the focus's name relation an invocatory force while leaving its prefatory ‘in the name of Allah’ construction intact.
findings.reader_payoff: The mercy titles can be heard as names through which the opening turns toward God, rather than as attributes only attached to the phrase.
findings.containment: The basmala remains an opening ‘in the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Merciful.’ The wider ayah supports an invocation resonance; it does not make 32:0 an imperative or identify al-Rahim separately in its call.

epistemic.reason: The focus analysis-to-QAC bridge is complete, and 17:110 supplies exact Arabic text. Target-side morphology is absent, so the contact is assessed at the supplied phrase level.

findings.title: Mercy with encompassing reach
findings.claim: The focus's paired mercy titles can carry an expansive divine reach: 7:156 states that God's mercy encompasses all things, while also specifying the people for whom it will be written.
findings.mechanism: The focus's two mercy epithets meet the explicit all-things scope in 7:156. This activates the branch's beneficent core and its divine-use facet of mercy reaching creation, adding breadth to the local mercy sense.
findings.reader_payoff: The opening's mercy can be perceived as reaching beyond one recipient or one act, with the qualifying continuation of 7:156 still audible.
findings.containment: The ordinary beneficent mercy sense remains intact. The broader text says that mercy encompasses all things and then names those for whom it will be written; the focus alone does not promise identical benefit to every being.

epistemic.reason: The focus bridge is complete, and 7:156 supplies the exact mercy wording. Target-side morphology is absent, so the branch contact is qualified at the phrase level.

findings.title: A question of the divine namesake
findings.claim: The focus's ordinary word for ‘name’ can carry an echo of the wider question in 19:65: ‘Do you know any namesake for Him?’ The opening's naming thus takes on a possible singularity pressure while retaining its ordinary designation sense.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies اسم as a name or designation. In 19:65, a direct question about whether the Lord has a namesake follows the description of His lordship and worship. The target's namesake relation contacts the focus's naming word and adds a question of unshared naming to it.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the divine name in the opening alongside a wider question about whether another shares it.
findings.containment: The opening still names Allah through its ordinary formula. The namesake question belongs to 19:65; 32:0 does not itself assert an answer or state that its titles are exclusive.

epistemic.reason: The focus bridge is complete and the connection supplies exact target Arabic, including the namesake question. Target-side morphology is absent, and the focus return is a phrase-level naming relation.
